To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the onset of ischaemia induced dopamine release in a slice preparation is controlled by the energy balance between energy supply (i.e., glucose) and energy utilisation (i.e., membrane Na+/K+ pump activity).
the onset of DA and/or glutamate release in this model of neostrial ischemia is controlled by the availability and utilization of metabolic energy substrates.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of neurotransmitter release in neuronal cell injury and the mechanisms that control release.
the effects of changes of energy demand and supply in the brain on the release of neurotransmitters.
the development and application of in vitro models to study the mechanisms underlying the release of neurotransmitters in ischaemia.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in this model of ischaemia, the onset of release of DA and possibly of other neurotransmitters, is controlled by the metabolic state of the tissue.
ischaemia induces an increase in the release of DA and that hypothermia slows this increase in the release, but does not prevent it.
, in the present in vitro model of cerebral ischaemia, the profile of DA release is controlled by the energy balance in the tissue.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the onset of DA and other transmitter release in this model of ischaemia is controlled by the energy balance between energy supply (glucose, O2) and utilisation (Na+/K+ ATP-ase).
the profile of neurotransmitter release in ischaemia is determined by the balance between metabolic demand and supply.
the onset of DA efflux is dependent on the balance between energy demand and supply, and that hypothermia may exert part of its neuroprotection by reducing energy demand.
The main takeaway from our work is that

strategies that increase the availability of energy substrated for the sodium pump (e.g., preincubation with creatines) or decrease their utilization (e.g., hypothermia) slow the onset of DA and other neurotransmitter release.
the profile of ischaemic DA release is temperature dependent.
hypothermia delays the onset of DA loss during ischaemia and that this may be one of the mechanisms by which it is neuroprotective.
